notes:
Scope: privacy before the modern era, antiquity to 1879 — the home as refuge (Cicero, Digest, Semayne, Otis, Pitt), confidential relationships (Hippocratic Oath, seal of confession), rules against looking and listening (Mishnah/Talmud, Qur'an and hadith, Blackstone), the fight against general warrants (Wilkes, Entick, Virginia 1776, Fourth Amendment), the sealed letter and the wire (1792 Post Office Act, Mazzini 1844, California 1862, Ex parte Jackson 1878), official data (census confidentiality), French 'vie privée' (1791, 1819, 1858, 1868), the watcher's view (Bentham) and the counterweight of public access (Sweden 1766), ending with Cooley's 'right to be let alone' (1879) as the hinge to the modern slice. Method: every quote was captured with tools/fetch-text.py and checked with --check (FOUND) except the Avalon Blackstone page, whose
-formatted text the helper's extractor skips; that quote was checked against the same fetched HTML with the helper's own norm() and matched, but is marked PENDING because --check itself cannot confirm it (the event also carries a CONFIRMED Supreme Court source). JSON APIs (Sefaria, quran.com, HathiTrust) were read where the human pages are JavaScript-rendered. Blocked sites (sunnah.com, founders.archives.gov, UCL, Gallica, BAILII, HathiTrust full text, OpenEdition, Oxford Reference, Britannica) were replaced by Internet Archive snapshots or by other copies of the same text; where no copy was readable the gap is stated below. Not verified / gaps: (1) the primary texts of the 1819 Royer-Collard speech and the 11 May 1868 press law (Gallica 403) — both rest on J.-L. Halpérin's article; the 500-franc fine in art. 11 of 1868 is therefore omitted. (2) The 1862 California telegraph statute text — the event rests on a Smithsonian interview with historian Brian Hochman. (3) Britain's Post Office Act 1710 is not on legislation.gov.uk; its letter-opening warrant power appears here only through Sir James Graham's 1844 statement in Hansard. (4) Cooley's 1879 first edition is behind a bot wall; the sentence is quoted from the 1906 edition at the first edition's star page [*29]. (5) Hippocratic Oath date is disputed (c. 400 BCE traditional vs Hellenistic). (6) Several locations are representative rather than documented (Kos, Sepphoris, Dublin publisher, Washington census office, Sacramento) — see each locationNote. (7) Non-Western coverage is limited to Jewish and Islamic law; no properly sourced pre-modern Chinese or Indian privacy norm was captured in this pass (Kautilya's Arthashastra, a manual of state espionage, is a candidate counterpoint). (8) The 'Hammurabi's Code protected privacy' myth was checked but no citable instance of the claim was found, so it is not recorded; the Code's house-breaking laws concern burglary, not observation or disclosure. (9) Semayne's Case is dated 1604 by Scalia J. and many sources, 1603 by others (regnal-year reckoning).

events.title: The Hippocratic Oath binds physicians to keep what they see and hear secret
events.place: Kos, Dodecanese (home of the Asclepiad medical families)
events.summary: The Greek Oath attributed to Hippocrates ends its list of duties with a promise that whatever the physician sees or hears in the lives of patients, in practice or not, and which ought not to be spoken of outside, will be kept secret as private. Its date and authorship are uncertain: it has long been placed at the end of the fifth or start of the fourth century BCE, but some scholars argue for a Hellenistic origin.
events.significance: The oldest widely known professional duty of confidentiality: information entrusted in a relationship stays inside it — a norm set by the practitioner, not the patient.

events.title: Cicero calls the citizen's home the most sacred place in Rome
events.place: Rome — speech before the College of Pontiffs
events.summary: After returning from exile in 57 BCE, Cicero argued before Rome's pontiffs that his Palatine house, demolished by Clodius, must be restored to him. In the speech De domo sua he asked what was more sacred or more hedged about by religion than each citizen's home, calling it a refuge so holy that no one may lawfully be dragged from it.
events.significance: A founding text for the idea that the home is an inviolable refuge — privacy imagined as walls and thresholds.

sources.institution: The Latin Library
sources.title: M. Tullius Cicero, De domo sua ad pontifices oratio, §109 (Latin text)
sources.quote: Quid est sanctius, quid omni religione munitius quam domus unius cuiusque civium? Hic arae sunt, hic foci, hic di penates, hic sacra, religiones, caerimoniae continentur; hoc perfugium est ita sanctum omnibus ut inde abripi neminem fas sit.
sources.note: Our translation: 'What is more sacred, what more hedged about by every kind of religious sanction, than the home of each citizen? Here are his altars, his hearth, his household gods, his sacred rites and ceremonies; this refuge is so holy to all that it is unlawful to drag anyone from it.'

sources.title: Gillian E. McIntosh, 'There's No Place (Not) Like Home: Domestic Space and Political Identity in Cicero's de domo sua'
sources.quote: In 57, once he had returned, Cicero delivered the de domo sua ad pontifices oratio before the high-priests of Rome; his objective was to have his house restored at public expense.

events.locationNote: Coordinates are the Regia in the Roman Forum, seat of the pontifex maximus; the exact room where the pontiffs heard the case is not given in the sources used.

events.title: Rabbinic law forbids windows facing a neighbour's window and names 'damage by sight'
events.place: Galilee, Roman Palestine (Mishnah); academies of Babylonia (Talmud)
events.summary: The Mishnah, compiled by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi around 200 CE, bars a person from opening an entrance opposite another's entrance, or a window opposite another's window, onto a courtyard shared by partners, so that residents keep a measure of privacy (Bava Batra 3:7). The Babylonian Talmud's tractate Bava Batra opens (2b) by asking whether hezek re'iyah counts as legal damage. Hezek re'iyah is the harm of being exposed to others' gaze in one's own private domain. Later (59b), in a dispute over a ledge overlooking a neighbour's courtyard, the Gemara says both disputing sages agree that damage caused by sight is damage.
events.significance: Treats unwanted observation itself as an injury with a remedy (a wall, a parapet, a blocked window), long before any Western privacy tort.

events.title: Justinian's Digest preserves the rule that a home is each person's safest refuge
events.place: Constantinople (imperial court of Justinian I)
events.summary: The Digest, published on 16 December 533 under the emperor Justinian, includes a passage from the jurist Gaius's commentary on the Twelve Tables (Digest 2.4.18): most authorities held that no one may be summoned to court from his own house, because a house is everyone's safest refuge and shelter, and whoever summons him from it is deemed to use force. The Latin maxim later reappears in Coke's report of Semayne's Case (1604).
events.significance: The Roman-law root of the 'castle' idea that English and American law would turn into rules about entry and search.

sources.note: Our translation: 'Most have held that no one may be summoned to court from his own house, because a house is for everyone the safest refuge and shelter, and whoever summons someone from it is considered to use force.'

events.title: The Qur'an forbids spying and entering others' homes without permission
events.place: Medina (the Prophet's Mosque)
events.summary: Two Medinan passages of the Qur'an set household privacy rules: 24:27 tells believers not to enter houses other than their own until they have sought welcome and greeted the occupants, and 49:12 says 'do not spy' on one another. A hadith collected by al-Bukhari ties the permission rule to the eye: a man who peeped through a hole into the Prophet's dwelling was told that asking permission to enter was enjoined because of that sight.
events.significance: A religious-legal tradition in which the ban on looking and entering without consent comes from the household's right, not from the state's grace.

events.title: The Fourth Lateran Council binds the whole Church to yearly confession and the confessional seal
events.place: Lateran Basilica, Rome
events.summary: Canon 21 of the Fourth Lateran Council required all the faithful of either sex who had reached the age of discernment to confess their sins to their own priest at least once a year. The council's constitutions were read and approved at its third session on 30 November 1215. The same canon ordered the priest never to betray the penitent 'by word or sign or in any other way', on pain of deposition and confinement to a strict monastery for perpetual penance. The duty of secrecy was older: Gratian's twelfth-century Decretum already ordered the deposition of a priest who revealed a penitent's sins. Canon 21 restated it as a conciliar decree binding on the whole Latin Church and fixed its penalty.
events.significance: A mass-disclosure system paired with a strict, enforced duty of secrecy — an early rule that compelled confidences must be protected by the institution that collects them.

For if anyone presumes to reveal a sin disclosed to him in confession, we decree that he is not only to be deposed from his priestly office but also to be confined to a strict monastery to do perpetual penance.

events.title: Semayne's Case: 'the house of every one is to him as his castle and fortress'
events.place: Court of King's Bench, Westminster Hall, London
events.summary: In Semayne v Gresham the Court of King's Bench resolved that when the Crown is a party a sheriff may break into a house to execute its process, but only after announcing why he has come and asking for the doors to be opened; and that a house is a castle only for its owner, not for others who take refuge in it. Edward Coke's report of the case begins with the resolution that the house of every one is to him as his castle and fortress, for defence and for repose.
events.significance: Turns the home-as-refuge maxim into a working limit on officers of the state — the 'walls' model of privacy in its classic legal form.

events.title: James Otis argues against general 'writs of assistance' in Boston
events.place: Council Chamber, Town House (now the Old State House), Boston
events.summary: The argument over whether Massachusetts's Superior Court should grant customs officers general writs of assistance began on 24 February 1761. events.significance: Carries the English castle maxim into a colonial protest against open-ended search powers — the argument the Fourth Amendment would later codify.

events.title: Pitt attacks excise searches of private houses: 'every man's house was his castle'
events.place: House of Commons (St Stephen's Chapel), Palace of Westminster
events.summary: During the Commons debate on the cider excise in March 1763, William Pitt spoke against letting excise officers into private houses; the Parliamentary History records him saying every man's house was his castle. events.title: Wilkes v Wood: a jury punishes a general-warrant search with £1,000 damages
events.place: Court of Common Pleas, Westminster Hall, London
events.summary: John Wilkes sued Mr Wood, an official he accused of taking an active part when messengers entered his house and took his papers under a general warrant issued over The North Briton No. 45. Charging the jury, Chief Justice Charles Pratt said a discretionary power to search wherever messengers' suspicions might fall was 'totally subversive of the liberty of the subject'; the jury found for Wilkes with a thousand pounds damages. The trial ran from nine in the morning to after eleven at night.
events.significance: Condemns the warrant that names no one and nothing — the ancestor of today's objections to bulk, untargeted data collection.

events.title: Entick v Carrington: private papers are a man's 'dearest property'
events.place: Court of Common Pleas, Westminster Hall, London
events.summary: King's messengers acting on a warrant from the Earl of Halifax entered John Entick's house on 11 November 1762 and carried off his papers. Delivering judgment for Entick on Wednesday 27 November 1765, Lord Camden (Charles Pratt) held there was no law to justify the search. A newly published contemporaneous report by Edward Moore has Camden saying private papers are 'the only way of concealing a man's most valuable Secrets' and are 'his dearest property'.

events.title: Blackstone classes eavesdroppers as a common nuisance
events.place: Clarendon Press, Oxford
events.summary: The fourth book of William Blackstone's Commentaries on the Laws of England (1769) lists eavesdroppers — those who listen under walls, windows or the eaves of a house to pick up talk and then frame slanderous and mischievous tales — among common nuisances. They could be presented at the court-leet or indicted at the sessions, and punished by a fine and by finding sureties for good behaviour. Blackstone was recording an old offence, not creating a new one: his footnotes cite earlier authorities, Kitchin on courts and Hawkins's Pleas of the Crown.
events.significance: A common-law offence aimed at listening in, recorded long before 'privacy' was a legal term. The U.S. Supreme Court still cited Blackstone's passage when it confronted electronic eavesdropping in 1967.

events.title: France's first constitution protects 'actions of private life' from calumny

events.title: Bentham publishes the Panopticon, a building for watching without being seen

events.title: The Fourth Amendment secures 'persons, houses, papers, and effects'
events.place: Federal Hall, New York (where Congress proposed the amendments)
events.summary: The First Congress proposed twelve amendments on 25 September 1789; ten were ratified by three-fourths of the state legislatures on 15 December 1791. The Fourth guarantees the people's right to be secure in their persons, houses, papers and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures and requires warrants based on probable cause that particularly describe what is to be searched and seized. Virginia's Declaration of Rights of 12 June 1776 had already called general warrants 'grievous and oppressive'.
events.significance: Writes the anti-general-warrant lessons of Wilkes, Entick and Otis into a constitution, and lists 'papers' beside houses — information, not only places.

events.title: U.S. Post Office Act makes it a crime for postal staff to open letters
events.place: Congress Hall, Philadelphia
events.summary: Section 16 of the Act to establish the Post-Office and Post Roads, approved on 20 February 1792, punished any post-office employee who unlawfully detained, delayed or opened a letter, packet, bag or mail of letters entrusted to him with a fine of up to three hundred dollars, up to six months' imprisonment, or both. The same penalty applied to secreting, embezzling or destroying a letter that held no money or securities. Secreting or stealing letters that contained bank notes or other money instruments was punishable by death. Under section 18, letters still unclaimed after being advertised were sent as 'dead letters' to the General Post Office, where they were opened and inspected, and any valuable papers were advertised and kept for the addressee.
events.significance: Builds confidentiality into a national communications network by statute — the carrier is forbidden to read what it carries.

events.title: Royer-Collard: private life is 'walled in' and 'declared invisible'
events.place: Chamber of Deputies, Palais Bourbon, Paris
events.summary: In the Chamber of Deputies on 27 April 1819, during the debate on the de Serre press laws of May 1819, Royer-Collard defended the bill's rule on proving defamatory facts. Truth could be proved against officials over acts of their public functions, but not against private individuals: 'it is not permitted to tell the truth about private life'. His words — 'voilà donc la vie privée murée ... elle est déclarée invisible, elle est renfermée dans l'intérieur des maisons' — are 'famous' in the historian Jean-Louis Halpérin's phrase. Halpérin also notes that the expression 'vie privée' does not appear in the law of 17 May 1819 itself.
events.significance: The clearest statement of the 'walls' model: privacy as a zone that the press may not enter, whatever the truth.

events.title: Mazzini's opened letters expose Britain's secret Post Office interception
events.place: House of Commons, Palace of Westminster, London
events.summary: On 14 June 1844 Thomas Duncombe presented a petition from W. J. Linton, Giuseppe Mazzini and two others. It complained that their letters had been detained, their seals broken and the contents read at the Post Office. Home Secretary Sir James Graham replied that the Secretary of State had held power to detain and open letters since the reign of Queen Anne, and that Parliament had reviewed that power in 1837 and left it with the Secretaries of State. He admitted that a warrant had been issued for one petitioner's correspondence but refused to explain further. Historians have since shown that Graham signed the warrant for Mazzini's letters on 1 March 1844 at the request of the Austrian ambassador, Baron Philipp von Neumann. Both Houses appointed secret committees in July.
events.significance: A landmark public row in Britain over state interception of communications: lawful under a warrant, yet felt as a violation of the sealed letter.

events.title: The U.S. census stops posting returns in public and promises confidentiality

events.summary: From 1790 assistant marshals had to post copies of census returns 'at two of the most public places' in their districts for inspection. In 1850, when the census began recording each individual, public posting was dropped and marshals were told not to use the facts entrusted to them to gratify curiosity or expose anyone's business. The 1870 instructions went further: 'No graver offense can be committed by Assistant Marshals than to divulge information acquired in the discharge of their duty.'

events.title: The Rachel affair: a Paris court bans a deathbed image published without the family's consent

events.title: California outlaws tapping telegraph lines
events.place: California State Legislature, Exchange Building, Battery Street, San Francisco (session moved from flooded Sacramento)
events.summary: Sitting in San Francisco after floods drove it out of Sacramento, California's legislature passed 'An Act for the Regulation of the Telegraph, and to secure Secrecy and Fidelity in the Transmission of Telegraphic Messages', approved on 18 April 1862. Its section 6 made it a misdemeanour, punishable by a fine of up to $1,000 or a year in prison, for anyone outside a telegraph company to read or learn a message 'by means of any machine, instrument, or contrivance' while it was being sent over the line. The historian Brian Hochman calls it the earliest statute prohibiting wiretapping, written soon after the transcontinental telegraph reached the West Coast. He says the first person convicted, in 1864, was a stockbroker, D. C. Williams, who listened in on corporate telegraph lines and sold what he heard to stock traders.
events.significance: What historian Brian Hochman calls the earliest wiretapping statute: privacy of communications follows the letter onto the wire.

events.summary: Article 11 of the press law of 11 May 1868, passed as the Second Empire relaxed censorship, made any publication in a periodical relating to a fact of private life a contravention punishable by a 500-franc fine. myths.claim: The law of privacy goes back to 1361, when England's Justices of the Peace Act provided for the arrest of peeping toms and eavesdroppers.
myths.correction: The 1361 statute names neither peeping toms nor eavesdroppers. It lets justices restrain offenders, rioters and barrators, and take sureties of good behaviour from people 'not of good fame'. Later lawyers read those general words broadly: Blackstone's Commentaries (Book IV, 1769) says a justice may bind over 'eaves-droppers' under them. In 1960, opposing a bill to repeal the Act, the MP Peter Rawlinson called the repeal bill 'a modest charter for peeping Toms and eavesdroppers', and the Commons refused leave by 230 votes to 148. The privacy reading comes from later practice, not from the text.

myths.claim: In 1819 Royer-Collard declared that 'la vie privée doit être murée' — private life must be walled in.
myths.correction: The words are Royer-Collard's own, but not from 1819. In his speech of 27 April 1819 on the press laws he said, descriptively, 'voilà donc la vie privée murée ... elle est déclarée invisible, elle est renfermée dans l'intérieur des maisons' — so there is private life walled in. The maxim 'la vie privée doit être murée' comes from his speech in the 1827 Chamber debate on a new press bill, where he said he was repeating what he had said in 1819. He then limited it at once: private life should be walled in against defamation, not against the publication of indifferent or honourable acts. The press law of 17 May 1819 itself does not use the expression 'vie privée'.

La vie privée doit être murée, mais contre quoi? contre ce qui lui est ennemi apparemment, c'est-à-dire contre la diffamation'. Source: Barante, La vie politique de M. Royer-Collard, vol. 2. myths.claim: The Post Office Act of 1792 prohibited postmasters from opening mail without a search warrant.
myths.correction: Section 16 of the 1792 Act punishes post-office employees who 'unlawfully' detain, delay or open letters, with a fine of up to $300, up to six months in prison, or both. It contains no warrant procedure. The warrant rule came later, from the Supreme Court: in Ex parte Jackson (1878), relying on the Fourth Amendment, the Court stated that sealed letters in the mail can be opened only under a warrant issued on oath or affirmation, as for papers kept at home.

Section 16 of the Act (1 Stat. 232, Chap. VII, approved 20 Feb 1792) does punish 'any person, employed in any of the departments of the general post-office' who 'shall unlawfully detain, delay, or open' letters. The only uses of 'warrant' in the whole Act (NJPHS OCR text) are 'warrant of the treasury' and 'bond or warrant' in the list of money instruments in the same section, so 'no warrant procedure' is correct. The MISLEADING verdict fits: the ban on opening is real, the warrant condition is not in the Act. Wording is too strong: 'did the Supreme Court hold'. Ex parte Jackson upheld a federal ban on mailing lottery circulars. myths.claim: Hippocrates himself wrote the Hippocratic Oath, with its secrecy clause, in the fifth century BCE.
myths.correction: Authorship and date are unknown. The Hippocratic Corpus is thought to have had several authors, probably spread over several centuries. The Oath has usually been dated to the end of the fifth or the start of the fourth century BCE. Most scholars still place it in the classical period, and some think its core may go back to Hippocrates. But H. von Staden's study of its language found affinities with Hellenistic writings, and Cristian Tolsa (2019) proposes that its ethical paragraphs, including the promise of secrecy, were added later, between the second century BCE and the first century CE.
